line_texts: We report time-resolved photoluminescence microscopy of exciton transport in layered hybrid perovskite quantum
wells with butylammonium and hexylammonium spacer cations. By fitting the spatiotemporal evolution of the
emission profile with an anisotropic diffusion model that includes exciton-exciton annihilation, we extract
both the in-plane and the out-of-plane components of the diffusion tensor on the same sample. The in-plane
diffusivity exceeds the out-of-plane one by more than an order of magnitude and decreases systematically as the
organic spacer becomes longer. Our results identify the barrier thickness as the dominant control parameter for
interlayer exciton hopping and provide quantitative input for the design of layered optoelectronic devices.
content.text: We report time-resolved photoluminescence microscopy of exciton transport in layered hybrid perovskite quantum wells with butylammonium and hexylammonium spacer cations. By fitting the spatiotemporal evolution of the emission profile with an anisotropic diffusion model that includes exciton-exciton annihilation, we extract both the in-plane and the out-of-plane components of the diffusion tensor on the same sample. The in-plane diffusivity exceeds the out-of-plane one by more than an order of magnitude and decreases systematically as the organic spacer becomes longer. Our results identify the barrier thickness as the dominant control parameter for interlayer exciton hopping and provide quantitative input for the design of layered optoelectronic devices.

line_texts: Layered hybrid perovskites have emerged as a
versatile platform for studying excitonic physics in
two dimensions, combining large binding energies with
strong light-matter coupling [1, 2]. In these
materials the inorganic lead-halide sheets act as
quantum wells, while the organic spacer cations form
insulating barriers that confine carriers to a few
atomic layers. The resulting exciton binding energy,
typically E_{b}\approx200\,\mathrm{meV} , exceeds the thermal
energy at room temperature by almost an order of
magnitude.

line_texts: Despite this progress, the transport of excitons
across and along the layers remains poorly understood.
In-plane diffusion is usually described by a single
coefficient D , yet the structural anisotropy of the
lattice suggests that the diffusion tensor should have
distinct components D_{\parallel} and D_{\perp} . Direct
measurements of both components on the same sample are
scarce, because the out-of-plane channel is difficult
to access optically and is easily masked by
exciton-exciton annihilation at high excitation
density [3].

line_texts: In this work we combine time-resolved
photoluminescence microscopy with a rate-equation
model to extract the full diffusion tensor of a series
of n=1 and n=2 quantum wells. We show that the
in-plane diffusivity is roughly an order of magnitude
larger than the out-of-plane one, and that the ratio
depends systematically on the spacer length.

line_texts: Single crystals of the n=1 compounds were grown by
slow cooling of a saturated hydroiodic acid solution
and exfoliated onto fused silica substrates in a
nitrogen glovebox. Flake thicknesses between 50 and
200\,\mathrm{nm} were verified by atomic force microscopy,
and all samples were encapsulated with a thin polymer
layer before being transferred to the cryostat.

line_texts: Figure 2 shows the mean-square displacement of the
emission profile as a function of delay time for the
three samples. At early times the profile broadens
linearly, consistent with normal diffusion, and the
slope yields an in-plane coefficient between 0.38 and
0.57 cm² s⁻¹. The values are about a factor of two
larger than those reported for thick polycrystalline
films [6], which we attribute to the absence of grain
boundaries in our exfoliated flakes.

line_texts: The out-of-plane component is obtained from the
delayed emission that originates from layers adjacent
to the excited one. Because the emission profile along
the stacking direction cannot be resolved directly, we
infer D_{\perp} from the lateral amplitude of the signal
at long delay times, where interlayer hopping and
annihilation compete.
content.text: The out-of-plane component is obtained from the delayed emission that originates from layers adjacent to the excited one. Because the emission profile along the stacking direction cannot be resolved directly, we infer D_{\perp} from the lateral amplitude of the signal at long delay times, where interlayer hopping and annihilation compete.

line_texts: We have measured the full diffusion tensor of
exciton transport in layered hybrid perovskite quantum
wells by combining time-resolved microscopy with an
anisotropic rate-equation model. The in-plane
diffusivity is more than an order of magnitude larger
than the out-of-plane one, and only the latter depends
strongly on the length of the organic spacer.
content.text: We have measured the full diffusion tensor of exciton transport in layered hybrid perovskite quantum wells by combining time-resolved microscopy with an anisotropic rate-equation model. The in-plane diffusivity is more than an order of magnitude larger than the out-of-plane one, and only the latter depends strongly on the length of the organic spacer.

extraction, whereas thick barriers can be used to
confine excitons within a single layer. Future work
should address the temperature dependence of both
coefficients and the role of dark excitons in the
interlayer channel.
